analysis.one_liner: Tightens federal aid rules on for-profit colleges, requiring more non-federal revenue.
analysis.headline: The bill has sat in the House Education and Workforce Committee since June 2025 with no cosponsors and no committee action.
analysis.plain_summary: For-profit colleges today can collect up to 90% of their revenue from federal student aid and still keep access to it. This bill would raise that bar: schools would need at least 15% of revenue from other sources, and it would close accounting loopholes that currently let schools count their own loans to students and in-house "scholarships" toward that share. A school that fails for one year would lose access to federal student aid for at least two years, instead of just getting a warning as under current law.
analysis.who_benefits: Students at for-profit colleges, who are less likely to be enrolled in a program kept alive mainly by federal loan dollars rather than real demand, and taxpayers, who currently fund a large share of the for-profit sector's revenue and eat the cost when students default on loans that never paid off.

how_it_helps.text: Replaces the 90/10 rule with an 85/15 rule, so a for-profit school must draw at least 15% of its revenue from non-federal sources to keep participating in federal student aid [S2].

Closes loopholes in how revenue is counted: institutional loans to students, income-share agreements, and in-house scholarships generally no longer count toward the non-federal share, so schools cannot manufacture compliance on paper [S3].

A school that misses the requirement in a single year becomes ineligible for federal student aid for at least two years; under current law one bad year only results in provisional certification, and eligibility is lost only after two consecutive failing years [S2].
Requires the Education Department to report annually to Congress how much of each for-profit school's revenue comes from federal aid, making dependence on taxpayer funds publicly visible [S3].

analysis.who_pays: For-profit college companies and their owners, including private equity firms that back them, since a large share of the sector's revenue comes from federal loans and grants and the tighter standard and automatic loss of aid eligibility would shrink or end that stream for schools that do not comply.

drawbacks.text: A school that loses aid eligibility for one failing year loses it for at least two years, and some schools would close, leaving enrolled students mid-program and owing loans for credentials they may not finish; current law's provisional-certification step gives failing schools a one-year grace period [S2].
Even the stricter standard still allows a for-profit school to draw 85% of its revenue from federal aid, so the bill reduces but does not end the sector's dependence on taxpayer funds [S2].

The effective date is the second full award year after enactment, so students at noncompliant schools would have years of warning, but schools that cannot find real non-federal customers have little path other than closure or shrinking [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill addresses a real problem: federal student aid is a major revenue source for the for-profit college sector, and school failures there leave students with debt and taxpayers with defaulted loans. The main cost is concentrated on schools that survive largely on federal money and would lose their aid pipeline, with enrolled students at those schools bearing the disruption of sudden closures. The bill softens this with a lead time of roughly two award years before the rule takes effect [S3], and the annual revenue report gives advance visibility into which schools are at risk [S3]. On balance it shifts risk from students and taxpayers to school owners, which is the stated purpose.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee in June 2025 and has stayed there, with no cosponsors, no hearing, and no vote so far.

narrative.text: Rep. Steve Cohen introduced the bill on June 17, 2025, and it was referred the same day to the House Committee on Education and Workforce [S1].
No cosponsors have signed on, and the committee has taken no further action on the bill since the referral [S4].
Congress remains in session, so the bill is technically alive but has not advanced past the referral stage [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one has won or lost yet, because nothing has happened; for-profit colleges continue operating under the looser 90/10 rule and its existing loopholes while the bill sits in committee.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: for-profit colleges keep current rules

for.name: Rep. Steve Cohen
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and referred it to committee; has not attracted any cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and Workforce
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on referral in June 2025 and has taken no action on it since; no hearing or markup scheduled.

against.name: For-profit college industry groups
against.what_they_did: The for-profit college sector has historically lobbied against tightening the 90/10 rule and related revenue requirements, which bear directly on the sector's access to federal aid dollars.

sides.party_line_note: No votes have occurred; the only sponsor is a Democrat with zero cosponsors from either party, so no partisan shape has emerged.

industries.industry: For-profit colleges and their owners (including private equity-backed chains)
industries.note: Many for-profit schools collect the bulk of their revenue from federal loans and grants; raising the floor to 15% non-federal revenue and making a single failing year trigger a two-year loss of aid eligibility directly threatens that revenue stream. The public's interest is in not bankrolling programs that leave students with unpaid-off debt, which runs against the sector's interest in maximizing federal dollars.

analysis.trajectory: With zero cosponsors and no committee action more than half a year after introduction, the bill is very unlikely to advance in this Congress unless a bipartisan group of members signs on or the committee decides to take up 90/10 reform; similar tightening proposals have repeatedly stalled at this stage.
